name: Andorra
summary: Andorra is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement (in force 10 March 2007), so a coffin from another party state travels on the laissez-passer for a corpse issued in the country of death. Andorra has no jet airport: the coffin lands in Spain (usually Barcelona) or France and continues by road, and the Spanish or French entry formalities apply at that airport.
coffin: Strasbourg Agreement standard (Art. 6, reproduced in Andorra's official gazette): watertight coffin with absorbent material, either an outer wooden coffin (sides at least 20 mm) with an inner soldered zinc coffin, or a single wooden coffin (at least 30 mm) lined with zinc; for air transport, a purifying (pressure-equalising) device or guarantees of strength accepted by the departure authority. No separate Andorran entry standard is published.
embalming: No Andorran entry rule is published; the departure country's rules apply. Spain, the usual arrival point, requires an embalming or temporary-conservation certificate in its consular procedure for coffins from countries outside the Strasbourg and Berlin agreements.
consular: No Andorran consular permit is needed from Strasbourg states: the departure state's laissez-passer suffices and transit or destination states cannot refuse it. Andorra's competent authority for issuing laissez-passers is the Servei de Medicina Forense (Departament de Medicina Legal, attached to the ministry of justice and interior). From other countries, the coffin needs the Spanish consulate's Documento Unico for entry at a Spanish airport (or the French procedure if landing in France).
arrival: Customs and health clearance take place at the Spanish or French arrival airport (in Spain, the funeral company requests the Sanidad Exterior entry authorisation through SISAEX, then customs releases the coffin). An Andorran funeral director drives the coffin into Andorra. Confirm burial or cremation formalities with the Andorran funeral director.
private_aviation: Andorra has no airport usable by business jets. Plan the flight into Barcelona, Girona, Toulouse or another Spanish or French airport with customs and health services, and a road transfer by an Andorran funeral director. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket.
export: An Andorran funeral home prepares the body and seals the coffin. For Strasbourg states, the Servei de Medicina Forense issues the laissez-passer for a corpse once Andorran medical, health, administrative and legal formalities are met and the coffin meets the Agreement's conditions. Other destinations may require their consulate's approval. Shipments usually leave by road to a Spanish or French airport, where their transit rules apply. Confirm delays with the funeral director.

name: Austria
summary: A coffin entering Austria must carry a corpse laissez-passer (Leichenpass) from the competent authority of the place of death, or one issued by an Austrian embassy or consulate. Austrian customs check the Leichenpass and the coffin on arrival, including on flights from other EU countries.
coffin: Austria applies the 1937 Berlin agreement (BGBl. 118/1958) and the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement (BGBl. 515/1978): a hermetically sealed coffin, normally a soldered zinc inner coffin in a wooden outer coffin with absorbent material. If no Leichenpass is presented, customs inspect the coffin or shipping case for serious damage, opening marks, leaks or strong odour.
embalming: Embalming is not standard in Austria and no Austrian rule requiring it for incoming bodies was found; it is usually done only when the destination (or departure) country requires it.
consular: An Austrian embassy or consulate can issue the Leichenpass and helps organise the transfer to Austria, which must be handled by a local funeral company working with an Austrian one. Costs are borne by the family or insurer.
arrival: Customs clear the coffin when a Leichenpass is presented. Without one, customs release it only if the coffin is intact; if it is damaged or leaking, the municipal doctor decides on release in writing. Only licensed funeral companies may transport the body inside Austria; burial rules are set by each federal state.
private_aviation: Austrian customs apply the Leichenpass check to every body brought into Austria, not only to imports from outside the EU, so a private flight from another EU state still needs customs clearance of the coffin at the arrival airport. Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
export: The district administrative authority of the place of death (Bezirkshauptmannschaft or city Magistrat; the mayor in Lower Austria) issues the multilingual Leichenpass on application by the family or the funeral company, once the post-mortem inspection (Totenbeschau) is done, the death is registered and burial is released. Only licensed funeral companies may transport the body. Each federal state sets its own procedure and fees (e.g. Tyrol). The destination country may require further documents.

name: Belgium
summary: Belgium applies the Strasbourg Agreement, so a coffin from another party state travels on the departure country's laissez-passer in a sealed zinc-lined coffin. Transfers with Germany follow the 1937 Berlin agreement, and other countries fall under a 1947 decree with similar sealed metal coffin rules.
coffin: Strasbourg states (art. 6): impervious coffin with absorbent material, either a wooden outer coffin with sides at least 20 mm thick and a carefully soldered zinc inner coffin, or a single wooden coffin at least 30 mm thick lined with zinc; for air transport a purifying device (or resistance guarantees accepted by the departure state) is needed. Germany and other non-agreement countries (Regent's Decree of 20 June 1947): hermetically soldered metal coffin with about 5 cm of absorbent material and antiseptic, inside a wooden coffin at least 3 cm thick with watertight joints, screws no more than 20 cm apart and metal hoops.
embalming: No Belgian embalming requirement for incoming bodies was found; follow the departure country's rules. For bodies leaving Belgium, an embalming certificate is part of the usual file.
consular: From Strasbourg or Berlin agreement states the laissez-passer is sufficient. From other countries, ask the Belgian embassy or consulate whether a legalised or apostilled death certificate is needed.
arrival: The receiving Belgian funeral director handles the formalities with the municipality for the burial or cremation; confirm the local requirements with the funeral director, as funeral rules are set by the regions (Brussels, Flanders, Wallonia).
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
export: A transfer licence is issued by the federal public health ministry (FPS Public Health, Belgium's declared Strasbourg authority) on the basis of the death certificate and a medical certificate stating the body has no infectious disease. The coffin is sealed and verified by the police or a municipal officer, and an embalming certificate is normally provided; all documents travel with the coffin. The US Embassy notes that remains cannot ordinarily be sent before the third or fourth working day after death.

name: Bulgaria
summary: A coffin coming to Bulgaria travels with the local death certificate legalised by the Bulgarian embassy (or a death certificate issued by the embassy), and the Bulgarian mission assists with the transfer once relatives or an insurer have covered all costs. Bulgaria is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement; for bodies leaving Bulgaria, Ordinance No. 2 of 2011 requires a hermetically sealed metal coffin or a soldered and sealed sheet-metal-lined wooden coffin.
coffin: Bulgarian rules for incoming coffins are not published separately. For bodies leaving Bulgaria, Ordinance No. 2 of 2011 (art. 24) requires a hermetically sealed metal coffin with a filtering system, or a solid wooden coffin lined with sheet metal that is soldered and sealed, or a tightly closed transport container, with sawdust and a chlorine biocide or an absorbent mattress at the bottom. Confirm the standard for entry with the Bulgarian consulate and the airline.
embalming: No Bulgarian requirement is published for incoming bodies; follow the departure country's and airline's rules. Ordinance No. 2 of 2011 (art. 23) allows embalming and/or cooling (maximum 8 C inside the container) for long-distance transport. For bodies leaving Bulgaria, the UK FCDO lists an embalming certificate among the repatriation documents.
consular: The Bulgarian embassy or consulate in the country of death legalises the local death certificate or issues its own, and assists with the transfer of the coffin or urn once relatives or an insurer have paid all costs. The municipality of the deceased's permanent address then issues the Bulgarian death certificate on the basis of the document accompanying the body.
arrival: Not published in detail: arrival health and customs formalities should be confirmed with the receiving Bulgarian funeral director and the Bulgarian consulate. Funeral arrangements follow the will of the deceased or, failing that, the spouse, adult children, parents or siblings.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
export: Leaving Bulgaria: transport abroad requires a permit from the director of the competent Regional Health Inspectorate (RZI), on the model in annex 2 of Ordinance No. 2 of 21 April 2011. The coffin (hermetically sealed metal coffin with filtering system, or sheet-metal-lined wooden coffin soldered and sealed, or closed transport container) is closed in the presence of a state health inspector of the RZI. Transport is by specialised funeral vehicle only. Deaths from cholera, plague, typhus, typhoid, anthrax, infectious tuberculosis, CCHF, polio or a new dangerous infectious disease require sealed polyethylene bags inside a sheet-metal-lined coffin. The UK FCDO lists a local death certificate, an embalming certificate and a certificate permitting transfer of the remains.

name: Saint Barthélemy
summary: Saint Barthelemy is a French overseas collectivity, so French rules apply: entry of a body from abroad is authorised by the French embassy or consulate in the country of departure, and an airtight (metal-lined) coffin is mandatory for air transport.
coffin: For air transport an airtight coffin (metal box) is mandatory under French rules. Confirm the exact coffin specification with the French consulate and the funeral homes.
embalming: France does not impose a single rule for incoming bodies; embalming or conservation care is normally required by the departure country and by carriers. Confirm with the consulate.
consular: The French embassy or consulate in the country of death authorises entry of the body into French territory; the funeral home handles the procedures. France is a party to the Strasbourg Agreement; whether a laissez-passer from another party state is accepted for Saint-Barthelemy should be confirmed with the consulate. Families bear all costs (insurance may cover them).
arrival: The receiving funeral home takes charge at the airport and arranges the funeral; confirm local burial or cremation deadlines with it. Transport from the collectivity to mainland France is authorised by the representative of the State in the collectivity, and transport from mainland France to the collectivity by the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long and heavy once metal-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Saint-Barthelemy airport has a very short runway restricted to small aircraft, so most jets cannot land there; plan a transfer via a larger nearby airport and confirm aircraft suitability with operations. The French airtight coffin rule applies to any air transport.
export: To send a body out of French territory, the funeral home obtains authorisation from the State's representative (prefect) for the place where the coffin is closed; for this collectivity confirm the competent State representative locally. An airtight coffin (metal box) is mandatory for air transport, and the destination country's consular requirements also apply.

name: Brazil
summary: Under ANVISA resolution RDC 662/2022, human remains must have been preserved (embalming or formalinisation), with a signed conservation record, travel in a sealed zinc-lined (or equivalent) impermeable wooden urn without a window, and be carried in the cargo compartment. Check with the Brazilian consulate which transfer documents, legalisation or apostille it requires.
coffin: RDC 662/2022 defines the funeral urn as an outer wooden box lined inside with zinc sheets or an equivalent material, impermeable and without a viewing window. The ANVISA conservation record model states the remains are placed in the impermeable urn which is then sealed in front of the signatories (family representative, doctor, assistant and two witnesses).
embalming: Mandatory: remains must have undergone a conservation procedure (formalinisation, embalming or another method set by ANVISA or the Ministry of Health), recorded in a conservation record (RDC 662/2022 Art. 5 and 6). Conservation and transfer services are prohibited when death was caused by spongiform encephalitis, haemorrhagic fever or another new infectious disease designated by WHO and the Ministry of Health (Art. 8).
consular: Brazilian consulates can register the death and advise on the documents for the transfer; the exact list (including any apostille or translation) varies by consulate, so confirm with the consulate in the country of death. Brazil is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Repatriation costs are normally borne by the family or insurer.
arrival: ANVISA carries out sanitary control of remains at airports only in public health emergencies or risk situations (Art. 3), but the documents must be available whenever requested (Art. 4). A Brazilian funeral company receives the urn, clears customs and arranges burial or cremation under municipal rules. Ashes are not subject to sanitary control.
private_aviation: RDC 662/2022 Art. 5 requires human remains to travel in the cargo compartment of the means of transport. Many business jets have no hold able to take a zinc-lined coffin, so check with the operator and ANVISA (port, airport and border health service at the arrival airport) before booking: the casket travels in the cargo hold, usually of an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650. Keep the conservation record and all documents on board.
export: A Brazilian funeral company arranges conservation (embalming or formalinisation) with the ANVISA conservation record, the zinc-lined urn, the notary-issued death certificate and a Federal Police authorisation document, and meets the destination country's consular requirements. Autopsy results can take a few weeks and cremation needs a judge's approval.

name: Switzerland
summary: Switzerland is a party to the Strasbourg Agreement and the 1937 Berlin agreement, so a coffin from another party state travels on the departure country's laissez-passer in a sealed zinc-lined coffin. Switzerland is outside the EU customs union, so the coffin clears Swiss customs at the arrival airport.
coffin: Strasbourg standard: an outer wooden coffin with a soldered inner zinc coffin, or a single zinc-lined wooden coffin, with absorbent material; the coffin may contain only the body and personal effects.
embalming: No specific Swiss requirement for incoming bodies was found; follow the departure country's and airline's rules. Bodies leaving Switzerland usually travel with an embalming certificate.
consular: From Strasbourg or Berlin states no consular step is normally needed. From other countries, ask the Swiss embassy or consulate whether legalised documents are required. Switzerland's declared treaty authority is the Federal Office of Public Health.
arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport, then the receiving Swiss funeral director arranges burial or cremation with the canton and municipality; rules and deadlines vary by canton. Cremation is the norm in Switzerland.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside. Flights from EU countries also need Swiss customs clearance.
export: Since 1 January 2025 the Leichenpass for a body leaving Switzerland is issued by the competent civil registry office (Zivilstandsamt), previously the cantonal doctor, based on an encoffining and sealing record from an authorised funeral director proving the coffin is sealed and contains only the deceased. The cantonal procedure varies (Aargau, Zug).

name: Costa Rica
summary: Costa Rican health law requires any body moved internationally to be embalmed and placed in an impermeable, hermetically closed coffin, with an official death certificate, a preparation (embalming) declaration, a sworn statement that the coffin holds only the deceased, and a transit permit. The receiving funeral home clears the coffin and must organise burial quickly, as burial normally takes place within 24-36 hours unless the Ministry of Health extends the deadline.
coffin: Executive Decree No. 1 (La Gaceta 69, 22 March 1968) requires the body to be placed in an impermeable coffin that is hermetically closed; for air transport the coffin travels in the hold of a passenger or cargo aircraft and may be fitted with a safety valve. The coffin must carry a fixed plate showing name, age, sex and final destination, and copies of the documents travel with it. Note: Costa Rica's General Cemetery Regulation (Decree 32833-S, art. 30) prohibits in-ground burial in metal coffins or other slowly decomposing materials, so a zinc-lined shipping casket may need to be replaced or placed in a vault or niche; ask the cemetery.
embalming: Required: the 1968 decree states that the body must be adequately embalmed. Costa Rica also requires an embalming certificate to send a body abroad (Decree 32833-S, art. 67).
consular: No published consular visa of the documents was found. Costa Rica is an Apostille party; to register the death of a Costa Rican abroad with the Civil Registry (TSE) the foreign death certificate must be apostilled or authenticated and translated by an official translator. Confirm with the Costa Rican consulate whether it wants to see the shipping documents before departure.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at the arrival airport (San Jose or Liberia), with the receiving funeral home collecting the coffin. Burial must take place 24-36 hours after death unless the Ministry of Health area office (Area Rectora de Salud) grants a written extension (Decree 32833-S, art. 29 as amended by Decree 42474-S); the funeral home should request this extension for a repatriated body.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the originals travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once sealed) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Costa Rican rules allow the sealed coffin on a passenger or cargo aircraft; no specific rule for private flights was found. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers (Juan Santamaria, San Jose, or Daniel Oduber, Liberia).
export: Leaving Costa Rica: international transport needs prior authorisation from the Ministry of Health area office (Area Rectora de Salud) on: a written request by a direct relative (or the embassy for a foreigner) stating destination and route; the Civil Registry death declaration form; a sworn statement that the coffin contains only the deceased; a medical stamp and a Red Cross stamp; and an embalming certificate (Decree 32833-S, art. 67). The 1968 decree requires embalming and a hermetically closed impermeable coffin. An official autopsy is carried out when a body is to be sent abroad, except for an obviously natural death of a person over 75 (FCDO). A temporary death certificate is issued first; violent or suspicious deaths involve the OIJ and a judge.

name: Cyprus
summary: Cyprus is a party to the Strasbourg Agreement; its competent authority for the laissez-passer for a corpse is the Director of the Department of Medical Services, Ministry of Health. A coffin from another party state travels on the departure country's laissez-passer in a hermetically sealed coffin meeting the Agreement's standard; rules for coffins from non-party countries are not published online.
coffin: From Strasbourg states: hermetically sealed coffin with absorbent material, as required by the Agreement (in practice a zinc or other sealed metal liner inside a wooden coffin). Cyprus-specific rules for incoming coffins are not published online; confirm with the receiving Cypriot funeral director.
embalming: Embalming is a legal requirement for repatriation from Cyprus. For incoming bodies follow the departure country's rules and confirm with the receiving funeral director; funerals in Cyprus are normally held within 24-48 hours of death.
consular: From Strasbourg states the laissez-passer is sufficient. From other countries, ask the Cypriot embassy or consulate whether legalised documents are needed; Ministry of Health rules for incoming coffins are not published online.
arrival: Customs and health clearance at the arrival airport; the receiving Cypriot funeral director arranges burial. There are no cremation facilities in Cyprus.

Land at a Republic of Cyprus airport (Larnaca or Paphos): the Republic treats entry through the north, such as Ercan airport, as illegal entry.
export: A local funeral director arranges repatriation: embalming is a legal requirement, and the funeral director provides the special casket and the documents, including a certificate of embalming. For Strasbourg destinations the laissez-passer is issued under the authority of the Director of Medical Services, Ministry of Health. Exhumation rules and typical delays are not published; confirm with the funeral director.

name: Czechia
summary: Czechia applies the Strasbourg Agreement and the 1937 Berlin agreement, so a coffin from a party state travels on the departure country's laissez-passer. From other countries, the Czech embassy or consulate in the country of death must approve the repatriation and issues the accompanying document (pruvodni list) for a 200 CZK fee.
coffin: A sturdy coffin with a zinc liner meeting the international agreements (Strasbourg articles 6 and 7: watertight, absorbent material, only the body and personal effects).
embalming: Embalming is not usually mandatory in Czechia; follow the departure country's rules for incoming bodies. Bodies leaving Czechia normally travel with an embalming certificate.
consular: From non-treaty countries the Czech embassy or consulate must agree to the repatriation and issues the pruvodni list in paper form, sent to the funeral service by post (fee 200 CZK in local currency). The foreign death certificate needs an apostille or consular legalisation so it can be registered at the special registry office (zvlastni matrika) in Brno.
arrival: The coffin is cleared on arrival with its transport documents. The body must be handed to a licensed funeral service, which arranges burial or cremation; for a Czech citizen, the foreign death certificate is registered with the special registry office (zvlastni matrika).
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
export: For a foreigner who dies in Czechia, the regional public health station (krajska hygienicka stanice) issues the pruvodni list (laissez-passer) required under the applicable agreement. For a destination outside the agreements, that state's embassy or consulate must consent, based on proof of death and confirmation of no criminal or health objection. On request and at the applicant's cost, customs can seal the coffin at the funeral home, crematorium or public health station and record the seal on the transport documents. The body is normally embalmed and travels in a zinc-lined coffin. Funerals must be ordered within 96 hours, though authorities normally allow more time for foreigners.

name: Germany
summary: Germany signed but never ratified the Strasbourg Agreement; it applies the 1937 Berlin agreement, under which a corpse laissez-passer (Leichenpass) from the departure country is the key document. Burial law is set by each federal state, and the receiving German funeral director handles local burial or cremation formalities.
coffin: Under the Berlin agreement: a hermetically closed (soldered) metal coffin, with absorbent material in the bottom, placed inside a wooden coffin at least 3 cm thick with watertight joints. Zinc is the usual metal; confirm any state-specific rules with the receiving funeral director.
embalming: No federal embalming rule for incoming bodies is published; follow the departure country's rules and confirm with the receiving German funeral director.
consular: German embassies and consulates can help with contacts to local authorities abroad. Whether foreign documents need legalisation, an apostille or a translation depends on the country of death; ask the German mission or the receiving funeral director.
arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport; the receiving German funeral director arranges burial or cremation. Burial and cremation rules differ between the federal states.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
export: The Leichenpass is issued by the local authority of the place of death (e.g. the public order office in Stuttgart, EUR 70), on application by the funeral company, with the medical death certificate, the civil death certificate and all documents required for a burial. If there are signs of an unnatural death or the person is unidentified, approval by the public prosecutor or a judge is required first. Under the Berlin agreement the body travels in a soldered metal coffin inside a wooden coffin; the rules of the destination and transit countries also apply.

name: Denmark
summary: Every body transported into Denmark must travel with a corpse laissez-passer (ligpas) issued by the competent authority of the sending state (Executive Order 152/1983). Denmark is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement but applies equivalent coffin rules; Nordic transfers are simplified.
coffin: Moisture-proof coffin with absorbent material: either an outer wooden coffin with sides at least 20 mm thick and a carefully soldered zinc inner coffin, or a single wooden coffin at least 30 mm thick lined with zinc. For air transport a pressure-equalising device with filter is required unless the coffin has a soldered zinc inner coffin and the body is embalmed. Transfers to and from Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden only need a tight, solid coffin.
embalming: Not required as such. For air transport, a coffin with a soldered zinc inner coffin needs either an embalming certificate or a certificate for an approved pressure-equalising device with filter; a single zinc-lined wooden coffin always needs the device. For incoming bodies the sending state's rules also apply.
consular: No Danish consular step is set by the regulation: the sending state's ligpas is the key document. The Danish embassy or consulate can advise on bringing a coffin or urn home; ask it whether the foreign death certificate needs legalisation or translation.
arrival: The death is reported to the parish (church) office, which also serves as the burial request; the receiving Danish undertaker arranges this. Burial or cremation generally takes place within eight days of death.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A zinc-lined coffin is about 2.2 m long and often 70-100 kg or more, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside. The Danish coffin rules for air transport (zinc inner coffin plus embalming, or an approved pressure valve) apply to any aircraft.
export: The ligpas for a body leaving Denmark is issued by the Danish Patient Safety Authority (Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed, which took over the former embedslaege role). The request form records the route and transport mode and the undertaker's attestation that the coffin meets Executive Order 152/1983 and holds only the body and permitted personal effects, with a soldering certificate for a zinc inner coffin and, for air transport, an embalming certificate or a pressure-equalising device certificate. Transport must start as soon as possible and no later than 8 days after death unless the issuing authority grants an extension.

name: Dominican Republic
summary: The Dominican consulate in the country of death processes the shipping documents: for a body, the original death certificate from the vital records office, a certificate of no contagious disease from the local health department, and a notarised embalming certificate signed by the funeral director or embalmer. The receiving Dominican funeral home clears the coffin at the airport.
coffin: Not specified on the consulate page. A hermetically sealed coffin is the usual international standard for air transport; confirm with the Dominican consulate and the airline.
embalming: Required in practice: the consulate's list for a body includes a notarised embalming certificate. The UK government also lists an embalming certificate among documents for repatriation out of the Dominican Republic.
consular: Documents are submitted to the Dominican consulate covering the place of death (the New York consulate publishes the checklist; tel. +1 212 768 2480, infony@mirex.gob.do). For cremated remains the death and cremation certificates must be apostilled by the US Department of State. Holders of a valid Dominican electronic ordinary passport are covered by a free repatriation insurance with Seguros Reservas (up to USD 9,000; notify Seguros Reservas within 48 hours of the death; 6-month waiting period for death from illness), per the Direccion General de Pasaportes.
arrival: Not published officially. The receiving Dominican funeral home normally handles customs and health clearance at the airport. Confirm burial or cremation formalities with the funeral home.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an international airport with customs and health officers (for example Santo Domingo Las Americas or Punta Cana) and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. No specific rule for private flights carrying remains was found.
export: To send a body out of the Dominican Republic, the death is registered at the Civil Registry office nearest to where it occurred; the death certificate is usually issued within 3 working days. All foreign nationals who die in the country undergo a post-mortem at the Pathology Institute in Santo Domingo or Santiago. The UK government lists the documents for repatriation as the civil registry death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. Dominican death certificates are in Spanish and do not state the cause of death; check whether the destination requires it.

name: Estonia
summary: Under the Estonian Cemeteries Act, a deceased person brought into or out of Estonia must travel in a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin filled with a desiccant, inside a tightly closed wooden box. Estonia is a party to the Strasbourg Agreement, so the departure country's laissez-passer covers transfers from other party states.
coffin: Hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin filled with a desiccant, placed in a tightly closed wooden box (Cemeteries Act section 3(2)). If death was caused by an extremely dangerous, highly infectious disease (yellow fever, viral haemorrhagic fever, smallpox, plague or anthrax), the body must first be wrapped in an antiseptic-impregnated shroud.
embalming: No Estonian embalming requirement found; follow the departure country's rules. The Cemeteries Act sets no fixed burial deadline but requires burial or cremation without undue delay.
consular: Estonia's declared competent authorities under the Strasbourg Agreement are the Ministry of Social Affairs and Estonian diplomatic missions. From non-party countries, ask the Estonian embassy what documents or legalisation are required.
arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport; the receiving Estonian funeral director arranges burial with the cemetery or cremation.

Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside.
export: Bodies leaving Estonia must be in a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin with desiccant, in a tightly closed wooden box (Cemeteries Act). A local funeral director must be instructed and works with international undertakers. A post-mortem is normally performed, always when death was not natural, and repatriation can go ahead once the authorities are content that no further examinations are needed. The death must be registered within 7 days. The authority issuing the laissez-passer is not published in English; the funeral director arranges it.

name: Spain
summary: Entry of a coffin into Spain must be authorised by Sanidad Exterior (Ministry of Health) at the point of entry, requested by the Spanish funeral company through the SISAEX electronic platform. From Strasbourg or Berlin agreement countries the mortuary laissez-passer is the only document needed; from other countries a Documento Unico from the Spanish consulate is required first.
coffin: A coffin suitable for international transport, hermetically sealed; the US Embassy notes a certificate of placement in a sealed coffin is issued for shipments. Simplified bilateral rules with France and Portugal apply to land transport only.
embalming: Bodies via the consular route need an embalming or temporary conservation certificate, and bodies leaving Spain must be embalmed or temporarily conserved. Embalming must be done 24-48 hours after death under medical supervision; embalmed bodies must be buried within 96 hours. A person who died of a contagious disease cannot be embalmed.
consular: From countries outside the Strasbourg and Berlin agreements, the family applies to the Spanish consulate in the country of death, which reviews the documents and issues a Documento Unico to be presented to Sanidad Exterior on arrival. From agreement countries no consular step is needed.
arrival: The funeral company requests entry through SISAEX to the Sanidad Exterior service at the entry point; once approved, the authorisation is downloaded and presented to customs for release. The receiving funeral director handles burial or cremation under regional mortuary health rules.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; they travel with the coffin and are shown to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. A sealed international coffin is long and heavy, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at an airport with customs facilities and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft airside. The Sanidad Exterior authorisation names the entry point, so the private flight must land at the airport declared in the SISAEX request.
export: The funeral company files the exit request via SISAEX with Sanidad Exterior in the province of death or of exit. The body must be embalmed or temporarily conserved and placed in a coffin suitable for international transport. For Strasbourg/Berlin destinations Sanidad Exterior issues the salvoconducto mortuorio; other destinations need their consulate's entry authorisation first. The US Embassy estimates 9-10 working days for an overseas shipment.

name: Finland
summary: Finland is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement (in force 15 March 1989), so a coffin from another party state travels on the laissez-passer issued in the country of death. On arrival, the cause-of-death documents go to the police of the deceased's home municipality (or of the burial municipality), and no separate burial permit is needed.
coffin: Strasbourg standard, reproduced on Finnish municipal laissez-passer forms: impermeable coffin with absorbent material, either an outer wooden coffin (sides at least 20 mm) with an inner soldered coffin of zinc or other self-destroying material, or a wooden coffin of at least 30 mm lined with zinc or other self-destroying material; for air transport, a purifying (pressure-equalising) device or guarantees of strength accepted by the departure authority. Finland's rule for coffins from non-Strasbourg countries is not published; the departure country's rules apply.
embalming: No Finnish entry requirement is published. The departure country's rules and the airline's requirements apply.
consular: No Finnish consular permit is needed for entry. The Finnish embassy or consulate in the country of death advises on burial, cremation and transport, and can receive notice of the death for a Finnish citizen. The death must also be notified to the Digital and Population Data Services Agency with the original foreign death certificate (which may need legalisation or translation).
arrival: When a coffin or urn is brought to Finland, contact the police of the deceased's last home municipality, or of the municipality of burial. The cause-of-death documents are handed to that police department, which may order an additional investigation in Finland if the foreign one is inadequate and establishes identity. No separate burial permit is required. The receiving Finnish funeral home collects the coffin.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights; the coffin needs the same documents as airline cargo. Finland is in the Schengen area: a flight from outside Schengen must land at an airport with border and customs control. A sealed international coffin is long and heavy, so it must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket.
export: The hospital or doctor issues the Finnish death certificate; if the death is unexpected, the police may order a forensic autopsy (the final cause-of-death certificate can take 4-6 months). Under Decree 226/1989 (amended 849/1993), the laissez-passer for a corpse (ruumiinkuljetuslupa) is issued by the health inspector designated by the municipal body of the municipality where the international transport begins (municipal environmental health services). It certifies the Strasbourg coffin standard and states the cause of death in English or French, by WHO code, or in a sealed envelope. A Finnish funeral director arranges the coffin and transport; confirm embalming needs with the destination country and airline.

name: France
summary: Entry of a coffin into France is authorised by the French embassy or consulate in the country of death, which issues a transport authorisation for the body. An airtight metal-lined coffin is mandatory for any air transport, and burial or cremation must take place within 14 calendar days of the body entering France.
coffin: For air transport an airtight coffin (cercueil hermétique, a metal box) is mandatory. Confirm with the receiving French funeral director in advance if cremation is planned after arrival.
embalming: No French rule specific to incoming bodies is published on the official pages; embalming depends on the departure country and the airline.
consular: The French embassy or consulate (with the Crisis and Support Centre where relevant) issues the authorisation to transport the body or ashes to France, and can transcribe the local death certificate into French civil status. It can give an indicative cost and contacts for local and French funeral directors. Families bear all costs. France has been a party to the Strasbourg Agreement since 10 June 2000.
arrival: The receiving French funeral director takes charge at the airport. Burial or cremation must take place no later than the 14th calendar day after the body enters France (CGCT art. R2213-33, decree 2024-790). The prefect may grant exceptions; a local derogation cannot go beyond the 21st calendar day.
private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. An airtight metal-lined coffin is long and heavy, so it must fit through the cargo door and into the cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. France requires an airtight coffin for any air transport, including private flights. A flight from outside the Schengen area must land at an airport with border and customs control.
export: To send a coffin out of France, the funeral company obtains authorisation from the prefect of the place where the coffin is closed. The same rule applies to EU and non-EU destinations. An airtight (metal-lined) coffin is mandatory for air transport. Ashes need authorisation from the prefect of the place of cremation or of the applicant's residence. The destination country's consular requirements also apply. The death is registered at the town hall (mairie), which issues the death certificate.

name: United Kingdom
summary: The UK has no import permit for a coffin. It must arrive with a certified English translation of the foreign death certificate and the foreign authority's permission to remove the body. In England and Wales the registrar then issues a certificate of no liability to register; Scotland requires approval from the Death Certification Review Service before burial or cremation.
coffin: UK law sets no specific import coffin standard. The coffin must meet the requirements of the airline and of the country of departure; confirm with the funeral directors.
embalming: Not required by UK law for import; the departure country or airline may require it. Tell the funeral director if a UK inquest is likely.
consular: No UK consular legalisation or entry permit is needed. British embassies can give lists of funeral directors but cannot pay costs. The UK is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: The UK funeral director collects the coffin. In England and Wales, take the foreign death certificate to the register office for the area of the funeral to get a certificate of no liability to register. Tell the coroner if the death was violent, unnatural or of unknown cause, as an inquest is likely. In Scotland, the body cannot be buried or cremated until DCRS has authorised it; DCRS aims to do this within 5 working days. Northern Ireland has its own process.
private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. For international general aviation flights, a General Aviation Report must be submitted online in advance through an approved method (penalty up to GBP 10,000). Arrive at an airport able to provide customs clearance and declare the remains.
export: To take a body out of England, the funeral director gives notice (Form 104) to the coroner for the area where the body lies, using the death certificate, the deceased's passport and the applicant's passport. Sealing takes place in front of the consular authorities, by appointment.

consular: The application is made in person at the Greek consulate with ID. The transfer certificate costs EUR 10 and is issued the same day once the file is complete. private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. A flight from outside the Schengen area must land at an airport with border and customs control.

name: Guam
summary: Guam is a US territory, so a casket arriving from abroad is subject to the same federal CDC rules as the US mainland (42 CFR 71 expressly covers Guam): the remains must be in a leak-proof container and, unless embalmed, travel with a death certificate stating the cause of death. A licensed local funeral home receives the remains after CBP clearance.
coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container (for example a casket with a leak-proof lining or a sealed metal transfer case). No territorial rule on zinc lining or witnessed sealing was found; the country of departure may impose a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin.
embalming: Not required by US federal rules for entry, but embalmed remains are exempt from the CDC death-certificate requirement. Remains of a person who died of certain infectious diseases may need a CDC import permit unless embalmed. Most departure countries and airlines require embalming anyway.
consular: No legalisation is required for entry. If a US citizen dies abroad, the US embassy or consulate can issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where no death certificate exists, a Consular Mortuary Certificate. Foreign-language documents need an English translation.
arrival: CBP clears the remains at the first US port of entry, with CDC requirements checked against the documents. Under 42 CFR 71.55 the remains must go directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. Under Guam law (10 GCA 3230), a permit issued under the law of any state which accompanies a body brought into Guam for final disposition is the authority to dispose of it, but the Director of Public Health may order a particular form of burial or disposition given the cause of death.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. An international arrival into Guam must clear US Customs and Border Protection, so plan the flight to an airport where CBP clearance can be arranged in advance and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. A flight from the US mainland is a domestic flight and needs no CBP entry, but the state burial-transit permit must travel with the remains.
export: Under 10 GCA 3230, no body may be buried, cremated or removed from Guam without a burial-transit permit issued by the Office of Vital Statistics (Department of Public Health and Social Services). The person first taking custody of the body must obtain it within 72 hours after death, and it is issued only after the death certificate has been filed. Permits for disposition outside Guam are issued only when the disposition complies with the Director's regulations. The destination consulate's requirements also apply.

A Honduran funeral home then clears the coffin on arrival.

embalming: An embalming certificate is required for the consular exit certificate for a body; cremation certificate for ashes.
consular: The Honduran consulate issues the Certificado de salida de restos mortales free of charge; at the Madrid consulate it is requested by email or in person without an appointment. The consulate does not register the death: a relative registers it with the RNP in Tegucigalpa using the apostilled death certificate. State-funded repatriation is possible only for families without resources, requested in person by a first- or second-degree relative, and only if the family has not already signed with a funeral home; it takes about 4-6 weeks.

No specific Honduran rule for private flights carrying remains was found; land at an international airport with customs and health officers with the consular exit certificate and originals.

For air transport, the body travels in a sealed metal coffin, or a sealed bag with a filter valve, inside a wooden coffin.

If the death was caused by a listed infectious disease, a soldered metal coffin inside a wooden coffin is required, with the body wrapped in cloth soaked in disinfectant. On the aircraft the coffin goes in the cargo hold, separate from baggage, unless a special aircraft is used, in which case the cabin may be used.
embalming: Not required by Croatian rules for entry as far as could be verified. The British embassy notes that embalming is not compulsory in Croatia but can be requested, especially for repatriation.
consular: The Croatian embassy or consulate issues the sprovodnica on the official form. private_aviation: There is no specific rule for private flights; human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as on an airline, and they travel with the coffin for customs and health checks at the arrival airport. Croatian rules allow the passenger cabin only on a special aircraft; on an Elysium Jet flight the coffin always travels in the cargo hold, separate from baggage, and must meet the sealed coffin rules.

The transport request must state the border crossing. A death examiner (coroner) issues permission to remove the body. The sprovodnica is issued by the sanitary inspector where the death was from an infectious disease or for exhumed remains. For air transport the body must be in a sealed metal coffin or sealed bag inside a wooden coffin. Non-infectious bodies not yet buried must be transported within 48 hours of death.

consular: The Hungarian consular officer issues the permit to transport a body into Hungary, applying Hungarian domestic transport rules. Hungary is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement. Fees and processing times were not published in the sources checked; confirm with the consulate.

name: Isle of Man
summary: A body repatriated to the Isle of Man must be notified to the coroner (the High Bailiff) of the place where it will finally lie, who decides whether an inquest is needed. The Island's government does not publish a specific import document list, so the departure country's exit papers and a local funeral director are needed.
coffin: No Manx coffin specification was found in official sources. Airlines and the departure country normally require a sealed, zinc-lined coffin in an outer wooden case for international air transport; confirm with the receiving funeral director.
embalming: No Manx embalming rule for incoming bodies was found; the departure country's rules and the carrier's requirements apply.
consular: No Isle of Man consular step exists (it is a Crown Dependency; the UK represents it abroad). British embassies and consulates can advise families on the local procedure in the country of death.
arrival: The coroner within whose jurisdiction the body will finally lie must be notified; the coroner then decides whether an inquest is necessary. After any coronial process, the registrar issues a burial order, or the coroner issues a cremation certificate. A local funeral director collects the coffin.
private_aviation: Fly into Ronaldsway (Isle of Man Airport) with customs available and the receiving funeral director meeting the aircraft. Human remains on a private flight need the same papers as airline cargo, carried with the coffin. The coffin (about 2.2 m, 70-100 kg zinc-lined) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
export: The coroner must be given written notice of any body being taken out of the Isle of Man and issues an Out of Isle of Man Order once satisfied with the result of any enquiries ordered. The death must normally be registered within 5 days at a civil registry office on the basis of the doctor's certificate of cause of death or the coroner's finding.

name: Iceland
summary: Iceland is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement, so a coffin from another party state travels on the laissez-passer of the country of death. Under Regulation 618/2018 on the handling and transport of corpses, every body entering Iceland must be in an airtight, watertight container inside a sturdy coffin and carry a packaging certificate and a doctor's certificate on contagious disease.
coffin: Regulation 618/2018 (art. 2): the body must be placed in an airtight and watertight container inside a sturdy coffin and secured so that it cannot move. In practice this means a sealed zinc-lined inner coffin in a wooden coffin. Iceland does not publish who must witness the sealing; the departure country's rules apply.
embalming: Iceland's regulation does not require embalming for an incoming body; follow the departure country's and the airline's rules.
consular: From Strasbourg Agreement states no Icelandic consular step is needed. From other countries, no Icelandic consular permit is published; ask the Icelandic embassy or consulate whether legalised documents are required. Iceland's Foreign Ministry consular service assists families of Icelandic citizens who die abroad.
arrival: Customs clearance at the arrival airport (normally Keflavik). If an incoming body has no certificate, it is handled under the procedures of the Chief Epidemiologist (sottvarnalaeknir) together with the district chief physicians. A body that may carry a notifiable disease is transported and kept under the Chief Epidemiologist's procedures. A local funeral director collects the coffin; Reykjavik's cemeteries run the main mortuary and two crematoria.
private_aviation: Fly to an Icelandic airport with customs (Keflavik, or Reykjavik for general aviation, to be confirmed with the handler) and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft. The same packaging and medical certificates apply as for airline cargo, and the coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
export: For Strasbourg Agreement destinations, Iceland's declared competent authority for the laissez-passer is the District Medical Officer (in Reykjavik, the Reykjavik Medical Office of Health), who may authorise staff doctors at health centres and hospitals to act (declaration of 4 February 1983). The body leaves in an airtight, watertight container inside a sturdy coffin with the packaging and medical certificates required by Regulation 618/2018. A doctor certifies the death and the National Registry registers it (Icelandic death certificates do not show the cause of death); a police inquiry or post-mortem can delay the release. Exhumation for transfer abroad needs a permit from the Chief Epidemiologist.

name: Jersey
summary: To bring a body into Jersey, a Jersey funeral director applies to the Coroner (the Viscount) for permission; the death must first be registered under the law of the country where it occurred. The Coroner may order a post-mortem on arrival.
coffin: No Jersey coffin specification was found in official sources; the departure country and carrier normally require a sealed, zinc-lined coffin for international air transport.
embalming: No Jersey embalming rule for incoming bodies was found; the departure country's rules apply.
consular: No Jersey consular step (Crown Dependency). For deaths outside the British Isles, the British consulate in that country can help the next of kin.
arrival: The Coroner may hold an inquest or order a post-mortem on arrival, taking into account any post-mortem abroad. The funeral date should not be fixed until the Coroner has decided. A Jersey funeral director collects the coffin.
private_aviation: Fly into Jersey Airport with the Coroner's permission already granted and the Jersey funeral director meeting the aircraft. export: Permission must be obtained from the Coroner before a body can be removed from Jersey in all cases. The Jersey funeral director completes the application, which requires a copy of the death certificate from the Superintendent Registrar (death registered within 5 days) and any further evidence requested, such as the passport. The funeral director must arrange reception in the destination and transit jurisdictions. Do not make travel arrangements before permission is given.

name: Luxembourg
summary: Luxembourg is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement, so a coffin from another party state travels on the departure country's laissez-passer; under Dutch rules, overland transport between the Netherlands and Luxembourg only needs the burial or cremation permit. For a death abroad, burial in Luxembourg is authorised in writing by the civil registrar of the commune, and must normally take place between the 24th and 72nd hour after death, extendable on a medical inspector's certificate.
coffin: Between Strasbourg Agreement states the coffin must meet the Agreement's requirements (leak-proof coffin with absorbent material, typically a zinc inner coffin in a wooden outer coffin). For overland transport between the Netherlands and Luxembourg, the Dutch rules require only a watertight coffin. Luxembourg's own coffin rules for other origins were not verified.
embalming: No Luxembourg embalming requirement for incoming bodies was verified; follow the departure country's rules.
consular: From Strasbourg states no consular step is normally required. Luxembourg missions (or Belgian missions where Luxembourg is not represented) can help families obtain or legalise local documents; repatriation costs are paid by the family, an insurer or a mutual association.
arrival: For a death abroad, the civil registrar of the commune of registration authorises burial in writing on the basis of the official information on the death that it judges sufficient. Burial normally between the 24th and 72nd hour after death; an extension can be granted on a medical inspector's certificate. Cremation rules for a body arriving from abroad were not verified: confirm with the commune.
private_aviation: Arrive at Luxembourg Airport (Findel) with customs, the receiving funeral director meeting the aircraft. Human remains on a private flight need the same papers as airline cargo. The coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
export: To send a body abroad to a Strasbourg party state, the laissez-passer is issued by the competent authority Luxembourg designated under the Agreement: Direction de la Santé, Division de l'Inspection sanitaire. Under Dutch rules, overland transport to the Netherlands only needs the burial or cremation permit. Delays were not confirmed; the funeral director handles the process.

name: Saint Martin (France)
summary: Saint Martin (France) is a French overseas collectivity, so French rules apply: entry of a body from abroad is authorised by the French embassy or consulate in the country of departure, and an airtight (metal-lined) coffin is mandatory for air transport.
coffin: For air transport an airtight coffin (metal box) is mandatory under French rules; in practice this is a soldered metal (usually zinc) lining inside a wooden coffin.
embalming: France does not impose a single rule for incoming bodies; embalming or conservation care is normally required by the departure country and by carriers. Confirm with the consulate.
consular: Under French rules, entry of a body from abroad into France is authorised by the French embassy or consulate in the country of death. France is a Strasbourg Agreement party, but whether a Strasbourg laissez-passer alone is accepted for this overseas collectivity was not confirmed: check with the consulate. Families bear all costs.
arrival: The receiving funeral home takes charge at the airport. Burial or cremation deadlines in the overseas collectivity were not verified: check with the funeral home. Transfers between the collectivity and mainland France are authorised by the State's representative in the collectivity (towards mainland France) or by the prefect (from mainland France).
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo, travelling with the coffin, and the French airtight coffin rule applies to any air transport. The coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Saint Martin shares its island with Sint Maarten; Grand Case airport is small, so many flights use Princess Juliana airport on the Dutch side: confirm customs and the transfer across the island in advance.
export: To send a body out of French territory, the funeral home obtains authorisation from the State's representative (prefect) for the place where the coffin is closed; for this collectivity that is the prefect delegate for Saint-Barthelemy and Saint-Martin (confirm locally). An airtight coffin is mandatory for air transport, and the destination country's consular requirements also apply.

name: Netherlands
summary: A body enters the Netherlands unhindered with the laissez-passer of the country of death (Strasbourg Agreement states) or, from other countries, a declaration from the competent authority naming the deceased and the destination; the document is shown to customs on entry. The civil registrar of the municipality of burial or cremation then issues the permit on that document.
coffin: From Strasbourg Agreement states the coffin must meet articles 6 and 7 of that agreement (impermeable coffin with absorbent material; confirm the sealing standard with the departure funeral director). From Belgium, Luxembourg and non-Strasbourg countries a watertight coffin is required (Besluit op de lijkbezorging art. 12).
embalming: No Dutch embalming requirement for incoming bodies; follow the departure country's rules. In the Netherlands embalming is generally prohibited, but the ban does not apply to bodies sent abroad.
consular: From Strasbourg states no consular step is needed. From other countries the declaration of the departure country's competent authority is required; ask the Dutch embassy whether legalisation is needed.
arrival: The laissez-passer, permit or declaration is presented to customs. The civil registrar of the municipality where burial or cremation will take place grants the permit on that document and keeps it. Burial or cremation normally within 6 working days of death; if the body arrives too late, as soon as possible after arrival. Transport by a hearse registered with the RDW.
private_aviation: Present the laissez-passer or declaration to Dutch customs on arrival, so use an airport with customs and have the receiving funeral director and an RDW-registered hearse meet the aircraft. The coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
export: The mayor of the municipality where the death was registered issues the laissez-passer for transport to Strasbourg states; for other countries a declaration of the competent authority naming the deceased and destination is used. If a non-natural death cannot be ruled out, the public prosecutor must give permission before transport, and embalming needs prosecutor consent. Embalming is permitted for bodies sent abroad.

name: Puerto Rico
summary: Puerto Rico is a US territory, so a casket arriving from abroad is subject to the same federal CDC rules as the US mainland (42 CFR 71 expressly covers Puerto Rico): the remains must be in a leak-proof container and, unless embalmed, travel with a death certificate stating the cause of death. A licensed local funeral home receives the remains after CBP clearance.
coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container: a double-layered, puncture-resistant body bag, a lined casket certified leak-proof, or a sealed metal body transfer case. No territorial rule on zinc lining or witnessed sealing was found; the country of departure and the airline may impose a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin.
embalming: Not required by US federal rules for entry, but embalmed remains are exempt from the CDC death-certificate requirement. Remains of a person who died of certain infectious diseases may need a CDC import permit unless embalmed. Most departure countries and airlines require embalming anyway.
consular: If a US citizen dies abroad, the US embassy or consulate can issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where no death certificate exists, a Consular Mortuary Certificate, Affidavit of Foreign Funeral Director and Transit Permit. A death certificate not in English must come with an English translation attested by a licensed official in the country of death (e.g. a notary).
arrival: Remains are cleared at the first US port of entry, where CDC import requirements apply. Under 42 CFR 71.55 remains for burial or cremation must be consigned directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory and, unless embalmed, accompanied by a death certificate (or an importer certification statement). Under Puerto Rico's Funeral Services Act (Law 258-2012), only registered funeral homes and funeral directors may receive a body into Puerto Rico, and the transfer and burial or cremation permit of a person who died outside Puerto Rico serves as proof of death.
pouch: For US/CDC entry purposes, a double-layered, puncture-resistant body bag counts as a leak-proof container. The country of departure, the airline or the aircraft operator may still require a sealed casket or air tray; confirm before the flight.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented at the arrival airport. The coffin must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. An international arrival into Puerto Rico must clear US Customs and Border Protection, so plan the flight to an airport where clearance can be arranged in advance and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. A flight from the US mainland is domestic and needs no customs entry, but the state burial-transit permit should travel with the remains.
export: Under Law 258-2012, a transfer permit (permiso de traslado) is required only when the body leaves Puerto Rico; it is requested by the licensed funeral director from the Demographic Registry (Registro Demografico) or Environmental Health (Salud Ambiental) of the Department of Health, and the body cannot leave before it is issued. Airlines and shipping companies must ask for this permit and for the documents required by the destination. Every body leaving Puerto Rico must be embalmed by a licensed embalmer, except for the US: embalming is not required there if the death certificate shows no contagious or quarantinable disease and the body is in a leak-proof container. For destinations outside the US, the funeral director must contact the destination country's consulate and meet its requirements. Bodies under the Institute of Forensic Sciences cannot be embalmed without its authorisation.

name: Portugal
summary: Portugal is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement (in force 8 August 1980), so a coffin from another party state needs only the laissez-passer for a corpse issued in the country of death. For a Portuguese citizen who died elsewhere, the consulate registers the death and issues an alvara de trasladacao (transfer permit) before the body can be brought to Portugal.
coffin: Strasbourg Agreement standard (Articles 6 and 7): hermetically sealed coffin (typically a soldered zinc inner coffin in a wooden coffin) with absorbent material, containing only the body and personal effects. Confirm the exact specification with the funeral homes and the airline.
embalming: No Portuguese entry rule found; follow the departure country's rules and the airline's requirements.
consular: The consulate covering the place of death transcribes the death into the Portuguese civil register and, at the family's request, issues the alvara de trasladacao. The Consulate-General in London needs no appointment for the alvara; UK certificates need no legalisation or translation there. For ashes in a wooden urn, the airline may require an alvara and consular sealing.
arrival: The receiving Portuguese funeral home collects the coffin at the airport and organises burial with the cemetery. Transport of a body outside the cemetery must be accompanied by the death certificate or a copy of the death record (Decree-Law 5/2000). No burial, cremation or coffin closing before 24 hours after death.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private aircraft was found. Portugal is in Schengen; a flight from outside Schengen must use an airport with border and customs control. The coffin must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket.
export: The death is registered at the civil registry; an international death certificate (Certidão de Óbito Internacional) can be requested. For Strasbourg Agreement countries the body travels with a livre-transito mortuario (laissez-passer), issued after checking medical, sanitary, administrative and legal formalities and that the coffin meets Articles 6 and 7 of the Agreement. gov.pt (April 2026) names the Public Prosecution (Ministerio Publico) as issuer, while Decree-Law 5/2000 gives this to the GNR and PSP police, so confirm the issuer locally. A post-mortem, if needed, normally takes place within 3 to 4 working days; cremation may need the public prosecutor's permission.

name: San Marino
summary: San Marino's law (Law 35/2010, Art. 16) applies international conventions it has joined to coffins arriving from abroad, and otherwise the rules of the departure and arrival states. The coffin lands at an Italian airport and continues by road, so Italian rules apply in transit; San Marino's civil registrar authorises transport after clearance by the health services.
coffin: San Marino's coffin rules (Law 35/2010, Annex 4): zinc inner coffin at least 0.660 mm thick, hermetically closed by continuous soldering, inside a solid wooden coffin at least 25 mm thick. For bodies from abroad to be buried in the ground, placed in ventilated niches or cremated in San Marino, the body must be wrapped before departure in a biodegradable, combustible covering inside both coffins so the zinc coffin can be removed on arrival.
embalming: No San Marino entry rule found; follow the departure country's and Italy's transit rules.
consular: No San Marino consular procedure is published. San Marino is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement. Confirm with the San Marino civil registry and with the Italian consulate whether Italian transit documents are needed.
arrival: Customs clearance takes place at the Italian arrival airport (Rimini or Bologna). A funeral vehicle must carry the coffin; transport within San Marino and burial need the authorisation of the civil registrar (Dirigente la Polizia Mortuaria), issued after the health services' clearance.
private_aviation: San Marino has no airport. Land in Italy (Rimini or Bologna are the nearest airports), where Italian customs and health rules apply, then transfer by funeral vehicle. A zinc-lined double coffin is large and heavy, so confirm it fits the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin).
export: Transport out of San Marino follows the international conventions San Marino has joined, or otherwise the rules of the departure and destination states; the civil registrar authorises it after the health services' clearance. For foreign burial, cremation or ventilated tombs a wooden coffin alone is allowed; where a metal coffin is needed it must be zinc (at least 0.660 mm). Transit through Italy is subject to Italian law.

name: Togo
summary: A Togolese embassy issues the authorisation to transfer the body to Lomé; the Berlin embassy requires the complete file at least 8 days before the flight. Togo's Ministry of Security also issues transfer authorisations (exit, and entry plus exit for transit).
coffin: The Togolese embassy in Berlin asks for the municipal authorisation to close the coffin but publishes no technical specification. Airlines and departure countries generally require a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin in a wooden case; confirm with the embassy.
embalming: Embalming is required: an embalming certificate is part of the embassy file.
consular: The Togolese embassy covering the country of death issues the authorisation to transfer the body (Berlin: 50 EUR normal, 70 EUR express, file due at least 8 days before transfer). Togo is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Documents in a language other than French may need translation; legalisation requirements are not published, confirm with the embassy.
arrival: No official description of clearance at Lomé airport was found; keep the original documents with the coffin and confirm clearance with the receiving Togolese funeral home. The family representative named in the embassy file is the contact in Lomé. For transit, the Ministry of Security issues an entry authorisation and an exit order. No national burial deadline was found.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains travel with the same documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health control; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. A zinc-lined coffin is large and heavy, so confirm it fits the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Plan arrival at Lomé-Tokoin (Gnassingbe Eyadema) International Airport.
export: Leaving Togo requires an authorisation to transfer remains (arrete de sortie) from the Ministry of Security in Lome: death certificate, cause-of-death or non-contagion certificate from the hospital, ID of the deceased and of the applicant, 500 FCFA fiscal stamp, online application on service-public.gouv.tg, processed in 72 hours and collected in person. The UK FCDO notes an export licence is needed, bodies sent to the UK must be embalmed, hospital death certificates may take about a week, and deaths outside hospital need a coroner's finding, which can take longer.
