name: British Virgin Islands
summary: To bring a body into the British Virgin Islands, submit the Application for Burial (importation and exportation of body) form to the Ministry of Health and Social Development with an authentic death certificate showing the cause of death and a burial permit from the Civil Registry; an approval letter and Importation Certificate (or a refusal) follows within two working days. There is no fee.
coffin: Not specified by the Ministry. A hermetically sealed coffin with outer case meets airline rules; confirm with the receiving funeral home.
embalming: Not specified by the Ministry; embalming is expected for international transport.
consular: The BVI have no consulates of their own; UK missions handle consular matters. No legalisation requirement is published; the death certificate must be authentic and state the cause of death.
arrival: Present the Ministry's letter of approval and Importation Certificate on arrival; the receiving funeral home arranges customs clearance and burial under the Civil Registry burial permit.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. Land at Terrance B. Lettsome International Airport (Beef Island) with customs clearance arranged and the Importation Certificate in hand; have the funeral home meet the aircraft. No specific rule for private flights carrying remains was found.
export: Leaving the BVI: submit the same burial application form in person or by email to the Ministry of Health and Social Development with the death certificate (stating the cause of death) and/or cremation certificate; an exportation schedule and permission letter are issued, to be collected within two days. No fee.

name: US Virgin Islands
summary: US Virgin Islands is a US territory, so a casket arriving from abroad is subject to the same federal CDC rules as the US mainland (42 CFR 71 expressly covers US Virgin Islands): the remains must be in a leak-proof container and, unless embalmed, travel with a death certificate stating the cause of death. A licensed local funeral home receives the remains after CBP clearance.
coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container (for example a casket with a leak-proof lining or a sealed metal transfer case). No territorial rule on zinc lining or witnessed sealing was found; the country of departure may impose a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin.
embalming: Not required by US federal rules for entry, but embalmed remains are exempt from the CDC death-certificate requirement. Remains of a person who died of certain infectious diseases may need a CDC import permit unless embalmed. Most departure countries and airlines require embalming anyway.
consular: No legalisation is required for entry. If a US citizen dies abroad, the US embassy or consulate can issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where no death certificate exists, a Consular Mortuary Certificate. Foreign-language documents need an English translation.
arrival: CBP clears the remains at the first US port of entry, with CDC requirements checked against the documents. Under 42 CFR 71.55 the remains must go directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. The receiving funeral home then handles the local burial or cremation formalities with the Virgin Islands Department of Health Office of Vital Records and Statistics; the territory's own requirements are not published online.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin), which rules out many light and midsize jets; an Embraer Legacy 600 or 650 is usually proposed for an adult casket. An international arrival into US Virgin Islands must clear US Customs and Border Protection, so plan the flight to an airport where CBP clearance can be arranged in advance and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. A flight from the US mainland is a domestic flight and needs no CBP entry, but the state burial-transit permit must travel with the remains.
export: Not published online. The Department of Health Office of Vital Records and Statistics registers deaths and works with funeral homes; a licensed funeral home normally obtains the death certificate and a removal or burial-transit permit before departure. For destinations outside the US, the destination consulate's requirements (embalming, sealed coffin, legalisation) apply. Confirm with the Office of Vital Records (St Thomas or St Croix).

name: Zambia
summary: Bringing remains into Zambia needs prior written consent from the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Lusaka, requested through the Zambian embassy. The body must be in a hermetically sealed casket inside a wooden outer box, attested by the local health authority.
coffin: Hermetically sealed casket inside a wooden outer box, attested by a notarised statement from the local health authority of the country of death.
embalming: The Zambian embassy checklist (Washington) does not list embalming. Airlines and departure countries usually require it; confirm with the Zambian embassy.
consular: Contact the Zambian embassy's consular section and send a scanned application package; prior written consent comes from the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Lusaka. No fee or processing time is published. Zambia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: The application must name the Zambian residents who will take charge of the remains. Arrival clearance details are not published; originals should travel with the coffin for customs and health checks.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains travel with the same documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs, immigration and port-health officers on duty; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. The zinc-lined coffin (about 2.2 m, often 100 kg or more) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Main international airports include Lusaka (Kenneth Kaunda) and Ndola.
export: The UK FCDO guide covers death registration (Registrar General, Lusaka, or local Boma offices; certificates in English, collectable within 48 hours), body identification and release from the morgue by the next of kin or a nominee. It does not detail export permits, embalming or coffin rules or timelines; the funeral director handles them. Post-mortems and police cases can delay release.

name: Zimbabwe
summary: A Zimbabwean embassy checks and stamps the original documents and obtains a health certificate from head office in Harare; the stamped originals then travel with the remains. Washington estimates about 5 business days.
coffin: The Zimbabwean embassy pages do not specify casket construction. Follow airline and departure-country rules (normally a hermetically sealed metal-lined coffin in a wooden case).
embalming: Embalming is required: an embalming certificate is on every embassy checklist.
consular: Send originals and copies to the Zimbabwean embassy (Washington: US$35 fee, about 5 business days, forwarded to head office for a health certificate; Ankara: US$10). If the deceased had no Zimbabwean passport, the embassy seeks clearance from Harare first. Zimbabwe is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: The embassy-stamped original documents must accompany the remains for clearance on arrival. Who collects is the family or a Zimbabwean funeral parlour; arrival procedures are not published.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains travel with the same documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs, immigration and port-health officers on duty; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. The zinc-lined coffin (about 2.2 m, often 100 kg or more) must fit the aircraft's cargo door and cargo hold (a coffin never travels in the cabin). Main ports of entry include Harare (Robert Gabriel Mugabe International), Bulawayo and Victoria Falls.
export: Per the UK FCDO, the death is registered with the Registrar General's Office (certificate within about one working week; BD12 medical certificate or BD11 police notice of death as applicable). Shipping requires the civil registry death certificate, a certificate of embalming and a certificate giving permission to transfer the remains. Rural mortuary facilities are limited.
